Build sheet: the sync watcher and the generated handover

Written by Intel, 2 October 2026, on Mark's tap: "Watcher plus generated handover." Ops builds. Intel audits. Nothing here invents behaviour; every rule below is a ruling.

Why

HANDOVER.md is the hottest file in all three vaults and the most conflict-resolved file in the estate's history: 178 commits and 10 distinct writers in Re.SOURCE over three weeks, 16 real merge resolutions, 10 of them in that one file. Two Re.SOURCE commit messages name the collision outright. Meanwhile the research found that git rejects a push at the ref level, not the file level, so two sessions pushing different files to the same branch still collide.

The fix is therefore not a faster push. It is removing the shared file from the sessions' hands and pushing on every write.

Deliverable 1, corrected after measurement: the post-commit hook, not a watcher

This deliverable was rewritten at 02:0x on 2 October 2026. The original brief was a file watcher on a timer. That is withdrawn, on measured evidence, and the reasoning is recorded here rather than deleted.

What the feasibility lane measured on this machine, in scratch repositories:

  • Two processes committing in one working tree: 40 trials, two at a time, 20 of 40 pairs had one side fail with fatal: Unable to create '.git/index.lock'. Six lanes over ten rounds: 50 of 60 commits failed. Roughly one in six succeeds.
  • Worse than the failure: lane A stages a.txt, lane B stages b.txt, A commits, and the commit contains both files while B's own commit then reports nothing to commit. That is silent cross-lane contamination, not a visible error.
  • A post-commit hook makes that specific window worse, because the hook holds the index lock for the whole network round trip. Measured push latency here is 0.14 to 0.50 seconds, so every commit serialises on a network call rather than on disk.
  • A watcher is a second writer to a tree that already has N writers, on a timer, with a stale snapshot of what to commit. It re-creates the collision above rather than removing it.
  • launchd is out on Apple's own words. WatchPaths is documented as highly race-prone, with no guarantee the file is in a consistent state when the job launches. A StartInterval agent polling git status is a third writer competing for the same lock, on a schedule nobody controls, possibly while a session is mid-rebase.
  • The folklore that fs.watch misses writes did not reproduce on this machine: 51 file operations produced 52 events covering 51 distinct files. The objection to the watcher is therefore not that it is unreliable. It is that it is a competing writer.

The corrected design, in four parts.

1.1 One worktree per lane. Measured cost of an extra Re.SOURCE checkout: about 94 MB against 195 GiB free, with the object store shared rather than copied. Ten lanes across the three vaults is under 600 MB. A worktree gets its own .git/worktrees/<name>/index, so index.lock contention disappears entirely. core.hooksPath is repo-level config and is inherited, with the tracked executable bit preserved, so the hook still fires. Git also refuses to put two worktrees on one branch, which enforces the one-lane-one-branch law mechanically rather than by discipline. What does not cross into a worktree: untracked files, ignored files, and anything a lane expects to find on disk, including .zed in the two vaults where it is ignored rather than tracked.

1.2 The post-commit hook, extended to all three vaults. Re.SOURCE already has one and its refusal to push on main is correct and stays. COMMAND and PERSONAL have no core.hooksPath at all, so only one vault in three auto-pushes today; sh .githooks/install.sh per clone is the one-time step and the file is already tracked. The hook pushes the lane's own branch, sub-second, with no extra process and no polling window.

1.3 One writer to main: the generator. main is reached by a single process, not by sessions. It fetches the lane branches, regenerates HANDOVER.md, commits and pushes. One writer means the hot file is rewritten by something that never races, and a rejected push is retried once after a rebase.

1.4 The never-fail sequence, validated end to end against a dirty tree, two remote advances and a real conflict. git pull --rebase before the commit fails on any unstaged file, which is the normal state of a live session, and --ff-only is worse: it succeeded against a stale origin/main and reported "Already up to date" while the remote was two commits ahead.

git commit -m "..."
git fetch -q origin \
  && git rebase --autostash -q origin/main \
  && git push -q origin HEAD

On conflict: git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U names the file, git rebase --abort restores everything, the commit stays safe and unpushed, the dirty edit is intact and the remote is untouched. Never --force: it succeeded in testing and would silently destroy a merged pull request. Never --force-with-lease: it reported "Everything up-to-date" when the remote had in fact moved.

Realistic pressure, so this is not over-engineered: all three repos are level with origin and nothing is unpushed. Over seven days origin/main moved under the local Re.SOURCE clone 9 times, all of them GitHub pull-request merges from arena branches, roughly one every 18 hours. There is exactly one clone of each remote on this machine, so local-versus-local contention is not the source. Expect single-digit rejections per week per repo.

The hazard that is already in the reflog, recorded so it is not repeated: on 1 October a session committed to main at 21:42:43 and at 21:43:32 ran reset: moving to origin/main, discarding that commit. It survived only because a work/zed-root-rule branch existed. This is the strongest argument for 1.1: on a worktree, that reset takes one lane's work with it and the branch is right there.

Deliverable 2: the generated handover

HANDOVER.md in all three vaults becomes generated output. One writer: the generator. A session never types it. This is the documented remedy for an unavoidable hotspot, single-writer serialisation, and it is the whole point of the exercise.

The rule for sessions, written into VAULT.md in all three vaults, replacing the current "overwrite HANDOVER.md with a fresh snapshot":

  • A session writes exactly one thing: its own note under the current week's _notes/.
  • The handover is built from those notes. If a fact is not in a note, it does not go in the handover.
  • A session that needs to change a rule changes VAULT.md, which is written by a person or a ruling, not by routine sessions.

Generator behaviour:

  • Reads the current week's _notes/*.md in date order, plus CARRYOVER.md, plus the estate health output, and emits HANDOVER.md in the existing three-part shape: Done, Next, Blocking. Keep the current shape; this is a change of source, not of form.
  • Never hand-edited content is preserved: if a line in HANDOVER.md is not produced by the generator, it is kept under an explicit ## Carried by hand heading rather than deleted, so a ruling written by a person is never silently destroyed.
  • Idempotent. Running it twice with no new notes produces no commit.

Deliverable 3: the console's first commit

Prerequisite for watching the console at all, and it carries a real security finding.

  • Write /Users/sushi/omo-console/.gitignore excluding shots/, drop/, .edits/, console.log, *.bak, .estate-lanes-cache.json, .estate-reading.json, and the literal directory named local:.
  • Exclude make-pair-qr.py. It contains a hardcoded 17-character password in the file itself. A secret scan across all 84 untracked entries found no other credential, so this is the only exclusion on security grounds rather than tidiness. Report it, do not commit it, and do not delete it without Mark's word.
  • Commit server.mjs, index.html, omo-acp.mjs, estate.mjs, shell.css, health.sh, preview.sh, send.sh, phone-links.sh, HANDOVER.md, ZED-GUIDE.md, shell-harmonisation.md, .zed/tasks.json.
  • No remote is created in this phase. Mark's tap on where the console's code lives is a separate decision and is not assumed here.

Deliverable 4: the lanes get their own worktrees

A small helper, so no session has to remember the incantation.

  • lane-start <vault> <name> creates git worktree add ../lanes/<vault>-<name> -b lane/<name> from the current main and prints the path. It fails cleanly if the branch or worktree already exists, which is git's own protection against two lanes on one branch.
  • lane-finish <path> runs the never-fail sequence above from 1.4 and reports PUSH OK or the conflicted paths. It never resolves a conflict and never forces.
  • Documented in Operations/Reference/GIT-WORKFLOW.md, which already carries the branch law that this makes mechanical rather than remembered.
  • The known limits are stated in the helper's own header: untracked and ignored files do not cross into a worktree, including .zed in the two vaults where it is ignored rather than tracked, so a lane that needs it must create it.

Verification, all of these must pass before this is done

  1. The hook in all three vaults pushes its own branch, and the elapsed time is measured and reported rather than assumed.
  2. Two lanes committing at the same time in two worktrees both succeed, ten rounds, no failures. This is the test the old design failed.
  3. A rebase conflict produces a stop, a logged path and an intact unpushed commit, in a scratch clone.
  4. The generator runs twice with no new notes, producing zero commits and a byte-identical HANDOVER.md.
  5. The console's first commit contains no credential, verified by a secret scan of exactly what was committed.

Out of scope

  • No branch protection. On a personal repository an actor can only be added to a bypass list if the repository belongs to an organisation, so protection plus no-bypass locks the owner out. Leave it off.
  • No merge queue. The research found it useful only for high daily PR volume, which this estate does not have.
  • No force-push, ever.
  • No rewriting the three vault VAULT.md files beyond the handover rule above. The Zed and OmO corrections in the audit note are a separate phase and a separate tap.
